titleEn: Guest article: The field day is the new term sheet; how growers are vetting ag robotics for real-use application
titleZh: 田间日取代投资条款清单：种植户如何实地考察农业机器人真实应用
summaryZh: 本文由UC ANR Innovate Connect项目负责人撰写，介绍了一种创新的农业科技创业公司评估方式——田间日（Field Day）。通过让初创公司在真实田间环境中向种植户演示技术，投资者可以观察到比路演更真实的团队能力信号，包括技术实力、客户服务意识和长期经营潜力。文章强调，这种实地压力测试比传统尽调更能预测创业公司的成败，已有公司通过参与获得商业合同。
featuredReason: 本文提出了一种创新的农业科技团队评估方法——田间日实地压力测试，对智慧畜牧领域的投资者和从业者具有重要参考价值，展示了如何通过真实场景验证技术落地能力，而非仅依赖商业计划书。
contentFull:
Connie Bowen is founding general partner at Farmhand Ventures, an early-stage impact investment firm that invests in agricultural technology focused on farmworker well-being, economic viability, and climate resilience. Hannah Johnson is founder of Hannah Johnson & Co. and industry lead at UC ANR Innovate.  Together, they operate UC ANR Innovate’s Connect program, a series of selective, free field days designed to get startups with real solutions in front of California’s farming industry.

The views expressed in this article are the authors’ own and do not necessarily represent those of AgFunderNews.

On August 6, more than 250 growers, investors, and startup teams from the US, Brazil, and Europe converged on a Connect field day to watch advanced physical AI technology take on one of agriculture’s hardest crops to automate: leafy greens. It was the sixth Connect field day we’ve hosted in just two years, with more on the calendar this fall and into 2027.

There are many factors to evaluate when investing in a startup. Most investors will agree that team is one of, if not the, most critical and controllable factors to analyze in making an initial investment decision. Markets shift, products fail, co-investors and customers change their minds, and at the end of the day, the people are left to navigate changing tides.

Unfortunately, it can be really hard to evaluate teams. Founders are always on their best behavior while courting investors, and they’re almost always going to make introductions to customers and partners with whom they have strong relationships. External reference checks can help, but we’ve found something better – pressure testing in the field.

Over the past two years, we’ve been working together to develop and implement the University of California Ag & Natural Resources (UC ANR) Connect program. Startups apply, get vetted by growers and researchers, go through virtual prep, then demo live at one of several field days hosted across California.

And what we notice after every cohort, in spite of all the vetting and prepping of these companies throughout the program, is that the field day tells us whether or not they’ll stay in business for the long run. The signals and data points that come from a company’s participation in a field day are invaluable in vetting teams, and too many investors are missing them.

We aren’t. And neither are most farmers. 

And the stakes are real. The founders who nail these signals don’t just leave with good feedback — they leave Connect with commercial contracts in hand. The ones who don’t, leave with a list of what to fix before the next one.

The clues investors can’t get from a pitch deck

We immediately clock how a startup staffs the event. When a company sends enough technical staff to answer growers’ specific questions, that tells us they value the opportunity and can support the work behind it. When one overwhelmed rep shows up, we ask why: they may be resource-constrained, or they may not understand what the opportunity demands. 

Afterward, we watch what happens next. Do they follow up with growers who asked questions, send the data they promised, and thank the host farm or research station? Those small acts are predictive because companies that treat a field day as a one-and-done PR stop rarely treat customers differently after the sale. 

The clearest signal is care: does the team ask growers real questions and listen to the answers—or do they see acreage instead of a person carrying the weight of feeding people for a living?

We get it — the economics still have to pencil, and none of these soft cues catalyze an exit on their own. But if the “there” doesn’t strengthen our food system or solve a real grower’s problem, we don’t care how good the math is. The win is short-lived, for all of us. 

We want more investors to see what we’re seeing — and act on it before the next cohort proves us right. We think you’ll be more successful, and agtech — and agriculture — will be better off too. With our next Connect field days already on the calendar for this fall and 2027, the smartest diligence you can do this year might be a day in the field.

translationZh:
8月6日，来自美国、巴西和欧洲的250多位种植户、投资者和创业团队齐聚一场Connect田间日活动，观摩先进的物理AI技术在农业中最难实现自动化的作物之一——叶菜类蔬菜上的应用。这是我们两年内举办的第六场Connect田间日活动，今年秋季和2027年还有更多活动排期。

评估一家创业公司时需要考虑很多因素。大多数投资者都会认同，团队是做出初始投资决策时最关键、也最可控的分析因素之一。市场会变化，产品会失败，共同投资者和客户会改变主意，最终，是团队在应对这些变化的浪潮。

遗憾的是，评估团队真的很难。创始人在向投资者示好时总是表现最佳，而且他们几乎总是会介绍与自己关系牢固的客户和合作伙伴。外部背景调查会有所帮助，但我们发现了更好的方法——在田间进行压力测试。

过去两年里，我们一直在合作开发和实施加州大学农业与自然资源系（UC ANR）的Connect项目。创业公司提交申请，经过种植户和研究人员的筛选，参加线上准备，然后在加州各地举办的数场田间日活动中进行现场演示。

我们在每一期项目结束后都注意到，尽管这些公司在整个项目中经历了层层筛选和准备，田间日仍然能告诉我们他们能否长期经营下去。公司参与田间日所传递的信号和数据点，对于评估团队来说价值不可估量，而太多投资者正在错过这些信息。

我们没有错过。大多数农民也没有。

而这些赌注是实实在在的。那些把握住这些信号的创始人，不只是带着好评离开——他们带着商业合同离开Connect。那些没把握住的，则带着一份清单离开，上面列着下次之前需要改进的事项。

**投资者从路演PPT中得不到的线索**

我们会立刻注意到一家创业公司如何为活动配备人员。当一家公司派出足够多的技术人员来回答种植户的具体问题时，这说明他们重视这个机会，并且有能力支撑其背后的工作。当只有一个应接不暇的代表到场时，我们会追问原因：他们可能资源受限，也可能根本不理解这个机会需要什么样的投入。

活动结束后，我们观察后续行动。他们有没有跟进提问的种植户？有没有发送承诺的数据？有没有感谢主办农场或研究站？这些细微的举动具有预测性，因为把田间日当作一次性公关活动的公司，在销售完成后也很少会以不同的态度对待客户。

最清晰的信号是关怀：团队是否向种植户提出真正的问题并倾听答案——还是他们只看到土地面积，而看不到那个以养活他人为生的、背负着压力的人？

我们理解——经济账还是要算得过来，这些软性线索本身并不能促成退出。但如果这个“团队”不能强化我们的食物系统，不能解决种植户的实际问题，我们不在乎数字有多好看。那样的胜利是短暂的，对我们所有人都是如此。

我们希望更多投资者看到我们所看到的——并在下一期项目证明我们是对的之前付诸行动。我们相信你们会因此更成功，农业科技——以及农业本身——也会变得更好。我们的下一场Connect田间日已经排在今年秋季和2027年，今年你能做的最明智的尽职调查，可能就是去田间待一天。
author: Connie Bowen and Hannah Johnson
